reasoning:
I'm planning out a Theo Jansen-style Strandbeest model: a wind-walking creature with yellow PVC tube framing, a central crankshaft, and multiple leg pairs built from rods approximating the Jansen linkage mechanism.

For the legs, I want to replicate the actual Jansen "holy numbers" (the proportional link lengths that make the mechanism walk realistically) and compute the joint positions through circle-intersection geometry rather than guessing coordinates, converting everything from centimeters to model units.

I'm trying to pin down the remaining joint distances for points D, E, and F relative to B, C, and O, but I'm not fully certain of the exact Wikipedia linkage values, so I'll settle on a plausible consistent set of distances to proceed with the approximation.

I need to make the circle-intersection solver clamp distances rather than return NaN when circles don't intersect, since different crank phases will naturally lift some feet off the ground while others touch down — which is actually authentic Theo Jansen behavior. I'll offset all legs by a shared constant so that the lowest foot across the gait cycle rests at y=0.

Working out the linkage geometry now with a scale factor converting the leg's native units to meters, defining each joint (B, C, D, E, F) via clamped circle intersections from the base points.

Still writing linkage code...

Working out the crank offset geometry: each leg's pivot O sits on the shaft at height H, with the crank center offset by fixed amounts in y and z depending on which mirrored group the leg belongs to, so that the two shafts stay coincident at z=0.

For the crank pin P, I'm computing it as the crank center plus a 15-unit radius vector at angle θ, with phase offsets spread across 8 slots for variety, and mirrored legs getting a 180° phase shift; I'll offset the x-position slightly for mirrored legs so cranks on the same shaft don't visually collide. I'm also planning the shaft as a thin yellow rod along x at height H, with short pin rods connecting each crank center to its pin point, and now I need to work out the actual leg lengths by estimating how far below O the foot should land.

Rather than hardcoding H, I'll compute it automatically: build the leg function relative to crank center at origin, find the minimum y across all phase positions, then set H so the lowest foot touches y=0. For the frame, I'm sketching yellow support tubes—a central x-axis beam near the pivots and cross tubes at the pivot z-positions, plus upper long beams running along z to complete the support structure.

Now I'm planning the upper structure above the legs: posts and diagonal braces connecting the cross tubes to the upper beams, plus a central ridge. For the sails, rather than modeling individual rows of bottles like the real Jansen strandbeest, I'll simplify to a central mast with a boom and an extruded cloth-like sail shape to suggest wind-catching panels.

I'm also considering added details like a row of pale blue bottles along the top beams, decal textures for the sail and bottle labels, sand-colored gradient paint at the feet, and weathered PVC coloring for the frame, then moving into writing the geometry helper functions.

Still writing geometry logic...

Now I'm defining helper functions for rods and joint balls, then planning the leg construction with mottled yellow coloring and dark ends. I'm also sketching the sail as an extruded outline in the y-z plane with a rough set of boundary points.

For the sails, I'm placing one on each side of the body offset in x, attaching masts as rods running upward, and defining the sail outline relative to each mast base with smoothed curves. I'm figuring out how to color them with stripes using paint based on position rather than textures or decals.

Now I'm adding bottles using a lathe profile for the body shape, arranging rows of them upright along the top beams on both sides of the structure, around 14 per side spaced along z. I'm deciding to skip label textures and keep things simple with just the geometric forms.

Working through the frame geometry now: placing upper beams at the correct height and lateral offsets, then figuring out post and diagonal placements connecting the cross-tube ends up to the beams, plus lower side rails running along z between the tube ends.

Now I'm adding the mast structure rising from the cross tube's center point up through the shaft, with stay rods connecting it to the beams, scaling the whole assembly down (~0.0085) so legs, sails, and mast height all stay proportionate. Setting up the rod helper calls to actually place these points...
